newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African apartheid minister wanted "more deaths".
newsitem.headline: S.African apartheid minister wanted "more deaths".

text.p: South Africa's former minority government approved a deliberate policy of killing anti-apartheid demonstrators on the advice of a hardline minister, according to newly released cabinet minutes.

The then minister of justice and police, Jimmy Kruger, recommended in August 1976 that police kill more black demonstrators as a way of crushing widespread anti-apartheid protests, the head of the state archive said on Friday.
Archive director Marie Olivier said in a telephone interview the recommendation was contained in cabinet meeting minutes released for publication on Thursday.
The minutes said Kruger had discussed the black student riots which broke out in Soweto township in June 1976 and rapidly spread to most other parts of the country.

"The minister proposes that this movement must be broken, and thinks the police should perhaps act more drastically and with a heavier hand, which would result in more deaths," said the minutes, written in Afrikaans and stamped "Approved".
At least 600 black demonstrators are believed to have been killed by police during several months of rioting in 1976, though some estimates put the figure higher.
The protests, originally sparked by government efforts to force blacks to use Afrikaans in school, were a major landmark in resistance to minority rule.

Thousands of black youths fled the country at the time to join exiled liberation movements such as Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which now rules the country after winning historic all-race elections in 1994.

Kruger, who has since died, was quoted in the minutes as having told his cabinet colleagues: "The danger is growing black consciousness and the inability to prevent the incidents (protests) because of the military precision with which the students act".

Olivier said current legislation provided for the automatic release of state documents after 30 years, but Mandela's government had approved the early release of the Kruger minutes after requests from newspapers.
She said outgoing president F.W. de Klerk had sought in vain before losing the 1994 election to have the 30-year period extended an additional 10 years.
No immediate comment was available from de Klerk, leader of the National Party to which Kruger belonged.
Olivier said Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission was not affected by the restrictions on release of government papers and had carte blanche to search state archives.
Mandela set up the commission last year to probe human rights abuses during apartheid in the hopes that disclosure and catharsis would help to heal the country's psychological scars.
No cabinet minister from the apartheid era has yet accepted responsibility for specific violations of human rights, though de Klerk has offered a general apology to the truth commission.
